title: Why I'm posting
post:
🚀 The last 4-5 months have been the most fun I’ve had building: 𝟮𝟯 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘀, from family care to disaster prediction.
Every 6 hours, I’ll share a new one: the problem, trade-offs and live link.

✨ What came out of it: live products across AI agents, family care, mental health, climate, education, sales, music, publishing and AR. Apps on Android and iPhone, 7 books on Amazon, and a music channel with 139 videos that runs at ₹0. Plus a 25-minute film made entirely in code and 12 browser games.

💼 Before building full time, I spent close to 4 years at Times Internet, growing from APM to Senior PM:
• Led the discovery, registration and acquisition journeys for the inaugural Times Internet Delhi Half Marathon: 18K+ runners
• Launched paid wellness subscriptions for Times Health+
• Scaled The Economic Times’ Assisted Sales revenue from ₹15L to ₹80L a month, and built AI TeleSuite for that team
• Unlocked ₹3Cr+ in incremental annual revenue with the ET Markets web revamp

Most recently, I ran D2C growth across the US, UK and global markets.

🧠 My learnings:
1. AI made building fast. Deciding what’s worth building is still the hard part.
2. Writing the code is now the easy part. Making it work on every phone, every edge case and every bad network is the real work.
3. People forgive an AI that says “I’m not sure”. They don’t forgive one that’s confidently wrong.
4. If a new user doesn’t get value in the first minute, they won’t come back for a second visit.
5. Building a product is half the job. Getting people to use it is the other half, which is why I’m sharing all 23 here.

⚙️ One more thing: these posts go out through a publishing workflow I built, and in the final post I’ll show you how it works.

Follow along, and tell me in the comments which product you’re most curious about. And if you try one and hit a bug, DM me. Every report helps.

title: LifeCycle-OS
post:
📈 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗟𝗶𝗳𝗲𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗲-𝗢𝗦: Enter any brand, get a full lifecycle marketing plan in seconds.
Built only on the brand’s real data: real prices, real ratings, real reviews.

🧩 The problem: D2C lifecycle teams have to ship emails, ads and landing pages for every cohort, in every market, every week, and every one has to be accurate and on-brand.

💡 The insight: lifecycle marketing only works when every message is built on the brand’s real data.

🛠️ What I built: LifeCycle-OS benchmarks a brand’s category, designs a complete lifecycle plan, then turns real customer data into on-brand mailers, ads and landing pages.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Real data only. Every price, rating and review comes from the brand’s own data, and anything missing is flagged “DATA REQUIRED BEFORE LAUNCH” for a human to fill.
• Brand isolation in code. One brand’s data can never appear in another brand’s campaign, and tests prove it on every change.
• Multi-brand from day one. Any brand onboards and the platform takes on its colours, voice and catalogue.

⚖️ The trade-off: some drafts come out with a gap for a human to fill, instead of a guess.

📊 How I’ll measure success: open and click rates on mailers, click-through rate and cost per acquisition on ads, conversion rate on landing pages, and the end goal: the sales each campaign drives.

💬 Your turn: What’s the hardest part of keeping your marketing accurate across every channel?

title: The Third Eye
post:
👁️ 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟮/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗱 𝗘𝘆𝗲: my take on JARVIS from Iron Man, built for everyday work.
One assistant that listens, sees, plans and acts across your tasks, notes, goals and files.

🧩 The problem: busy people run their day across too many apps. Tasks live in one, notes in another, email and calendar somewhere else, so no assistant ever sees the full picture.

💡 The insight: Tony Stark doesn’t open apps. He talks to JARVIS, and JARVIS uses the tools. That’s how an assistant should feel.

🛠️ What I built, mapped to JARVIS:
• Talks and listens, like JARVIS in the lab: live voice capture and spoken replies.
• Sees what you see, like E.D.I.T.H.: share your screen or webcam and it understands what’s in front of you.
• Runs the workshop: tasks, notes, goals and a life log, with “Run with JARVIS” to work through your task list on autopilot.
• Knows your files: a knowledge base built from your PDFs, Word, Excel and notes, checked before it answers.
• Handles comms: Gmail and Google Calendar, open to early-access users while Google completes its review.
• Builds on command: 28 studio tools across personal, startup and office work, from music and trip plans to landing pages, mailers, PRDs and OKRs.
• A suit for every mission: personas that change its tone and voice, and Personal, Professional and Enterprise modes.
• One hub: 24 tools I built plus 76 linked apps.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• It asks before it acts. Anything that changes the world, like sending an email, needs your confirmation.
• Every action is logged, with a kill switch, so JARVIS never turns into ULTRON.
• A business model from day one: credit packs paid through Razorpay.

🚧 Building now: an always-listening JARVIS (with your permission) that turns your day into tasks, reminders and fixes, finishes them itself, and lets you rewind any hour in the Life Log. One tap turns it off.

⚖️ The trade-off: I shipped a working product on a simpler architecture first. A fuller agent backend is built and tested, and deploys next.

📊 How I’ll measure success: daily and weekly active users, tasks completed through the assistant, apps connected per user, 30-day retention, and the end goal: credit-pack revenue.

💬 Your turn: If you had your own JARVIS, what’s the first thing you’d ask it to do?

title: Parwah
post:
👨‍👩‍👧 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟯/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘄𝗮𝗵: a family-care app for Indian families looking after ageing parents.
It ends the WhatsApp line every family knows: “I thought you did.”

🧩 The problem: siblings in different cities share their parents’ care through a family WhatsApp group. “Did anyone book Papa’s blood test?” Everyone sees the message. Nobody knows who’s handling it.

💡 The insight: caring for parents is a task problem, not a chat problem.

🛠️ What I built: Parwah (परवाह), the family superapp for what matters: papers, health, to-dos and an emergency card, shared only with family. WhatsApp stays for chat. Free for families.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Clear ownership. Every to-do shows who has it, like “Rohan has it, by Friday”, or that nobody has it yet.
• A readiness score shows what’s missing, like an insurance card nobody has added.
• Ask Ekta, the family assistant: “What medicines is Mum taking?”
• Papers, permissioned. Only the owner decides who can open an Aadhaar, PAN or passport.
• An emergency card with everything a doctor asks for, working with no internet.

⚖️ The trade-off: keeping things current takes a little more effort than a chat. The readiness score makes that effort visible and worth it.

📊 How I’ll measure success: families activated, needs closed per family each month, time for an open need to be claimed, weekly active family members, and the end goal: families who keep using it every week.

Apni family ki parwah karein.

title: LoosenUp
post:
🧘 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟰/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗨𝗽: a stress-relief app built for your worst 2 minutes, not your best 20.
Rate how calm you feel, take a short guided break, and see the difference it made.

🧩 The problem: when you’re tense or low, you need relief in the moment. But many wellness apps want a sign-up, a 20-minute session and a daily streak, and on your worst day you’ll do none of it.

💡 The insight: design for the worst moment, not the average one.

🛠️ What I built: a 2-minute guided break matched to what you’re carrying, with a before and after calm rating.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Value you can see. You rate how calm you feel before and after, and see your “Calm gain”.
• Safety first. An SOS button on every screen, even before sign-up, with Tele-MANAS 14416, a trusted contact and emergency 112. Distress phrases typed anywhere bring help forward.
• No barriers. No account needed, it works offline, and it installs without an app store.

⚖️ The trade-off: I chose short and simple over deep programmes. It’s a wellbeing companion, not medical care, and it says so.

📊 How I’ll measure success: breaks started, average Calm gain, how many people return within 7 and 30 days, and the end goal: people who open it again whenever they need it.

💬 Your turn: What do you do in the worst 2 minutes of your day?

title: Predict Natural Disasters
post:
🌍 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟱/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁 𝗡𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: a live global hazard map built on 8 official data sources.
Its best feature: it grades its own forecasts and tells you when it was wrong.

🧩 The problem: newsrooms, NGOs and operations teams need one trustworthy global view when disaster strikes, but the data is spread across a dozen agency websites. And many “AI predicts disasters” products make bold forecasts that nobody ever checks.

💡 The insight: in a high-stakes field, being believed matters more than being impressive.

🛠️ What I built: one live map combining USGS, NASA, GDACS, NOAA, EMSC, ReliefWeb and more, with experimental outlooks on top.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Every forecast is accountable. Each one states its evidence, its confidence and the time window it will be graded in, then it’s checked against what actually happened.
• Failures stay small. If one source goes down, coverage shrinks, but the map never goes blank.
• Silence isn’t safety. If no source covers a region, it says “not covered”, never “all clear”.

⚖️ The trade-off: fewer flashy predictions in exchange for more trust.

📊 How I’ll measure success: daily users, forecast hit rate against the rules declared upfront, source coverage and uptime, map views shared, and the end goal: newsrooms, NGOs and operations teams relying on it every day.

💬 Your turn: Would you rather have a bold forecast or an honest one?

title: Edu AI
post:
🎓 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟲/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗘𝗱𝘂 𝗔𝗜: an AI-first learning planner for a child’s whole education, from birth to Class 12.
Because today, no app a child uses knows what the last one taught.

🧩 The problem: from a toddler app to JEE coaching, an Indian child’s education passes through app after app, and each one starts from zero. Parents never get one clear plan from year to year.

💡 The insight: learning is one continuous journey, so the product should track it as one.

🛠️ What I built: one skill map aligned to NCERT and India’s National Curriculum Framework, from home learning at birth to Class 12. Competitive and study-abroad tracks branch from it, so nothing starts from zero.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• One map from age 0 to 18. JEE, NEET, CUET and UPSC tracks branch off it from Class 8-9.
• Grounded in India’s official curriculum frameworks, across CBSE, ICSE/ISC, NIOS and state boards.
• Zero screen time for children under 3. The product guides parents, not toddlers.

⚖️ The trade-off: I built the data foundations before a single lesson, because in education the structure is the product.

📊 How I’ll measure success: families onboarded, plans created, monthly active families, plans followed month after month, and the end goal: families who stay with it from one school year to the next.

title: AI TeleSuite
post:
A sales manager can listen to a handful of calls a day. Every other call goes unheard, and so does the coaching that rep needed.

📞 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟳/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗔𝗜 𝗧𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗦𝘂𝗶𝘁𝗲: an AI toolkit that listens to every sales call so managers can coach.
I built it at The Economic Times, where I scaled Assisted Sales from ₹15L to ₹80L a month.

🧩 The problem: in a growing Assisted Sales team, call quality depends on coaching, and coaching depends on listening. A manager can only hear a handful of calls. The rest go unheard, unscored and uncoached.

💡 The insight: let AI listen to every call, so managers can spend their time coaching.

🛠️ What I built: one toolkit that transcribes every call, scores it, including how objections were handled, and helps agents with the pitch.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Two versions in one product: a full version on paid AI services and a free open-source version, so it works on any budget.
• Built for internal use, with server-checked PIN access and a lockout, because call data is sensitive.
• Built inside the team that would use it. I didn’t guess at the problem. I lived it every day.

⚖️ The trade-off: a PIN-locked internal tool is harder to demo publicly, but call data has to stay private.

📊 How I measured it: share of calls scored, call quality scores over time, conversion rate per agent, and the end goal: the team’s Assisted Sales revenue, which grew from ₹15L to ₹80L a month.

💬 Your turn: Sales leaders: how many of your team’s calls do you actually get to hear?

title: Hey Yaara
post:
Some evenings you don’t want advice. You just want someone to say, “Haan yaar, samajh sakta hoon.”

🗣️ 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟴/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗛𝗲𝘆 𝗬𝗮𝗮𝗿𝗮: a Hinglish AI voice companion you can call like a friend.
“Yaar, aaj ka din bekaar tha.” Many AI assistants reply like a textbook. Yaara replies like a friend.

🧩 The problem: many voice assistants are built English-first. Many Indians talk in Hinglish, and an assistant that answers like a textbook feels like software, not company.

💡 The insight: for a voice companion, the experience is the product. And the worst experience is silence.

🛠️ What I built: a companion you “call” like a friend, in Hinglish by default, with a music hub and games for when you’d rather not talk.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Familiar sign-up: a mobile number and PIN, the way Indians already sign up for apps. No email needed.
• Fallbacks everywhere. If the AI model fails, a backup takes over. If the premium voice fails, the phone’s own voice speaks. The call never goes quiet.
• Private by design. Every call and transcript belongs only to its account, and access is checked on every request.

⚖️ The trade-off: building native apps took longer than the web version alone, but phones’ own speech engines make the call feel real.

📊 How I’ll measure success: calls per user, average call length, 7- and 30-day retention, app installs and ratings, and the end goal: Yaara becoming a daily habit.

💬 Your turn: Which language would you want an AI to talk to you in?

title: Animind
post:
Your dog has been whining at the door for ten minutes. Hungry? Anxious? In pain? You’re guessing, and guessing feels awful.

🐾 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟵/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗔𝗻𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗱: an AI that reads your pet’s state from a 10-second recording.
Not a “pet translator”. It tells you what the sound can actually reveal, and how sure it is.

🧩 The problem: pet owners can hear that something is wrong, but not what kind of wrong. And “AI pet translators” promise to decode words that animals don’t use.

💡 The insight: an animal’s sound reliably carries two signals: arousal (how worked up it is) and valence (distressed or happy), read from features like pitch contour and jitter. Build on what’s real, not what sounds magical.

🛠️ What I built: record 10 seconds, and Animind gives a plain sentence, the measurements behind it and an honest confidence level.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Clear positioning: not a translator, not a diagnosis.
• If a recording is too noisy, it says so instead of guessing.
• It compares against what’s normal for the species and for your own animal.

⚖️ The trade-off: modest, honest answers over magical ones that would go viral and then lose trust.

📊 How I’ll measure success: recordings per pet, repeat use each week, how often vets agree with the readings, results shared, and the end goal: owners who check in on their pet every week.

💬 Your turn: Pet parents: which sound from your pet do you wish you understood?

title: TH+ LifeEngine
post:
You finally got a diet plan from a chatbot. Two days later, it’s a forgotten paragraph somewhere in your chat history.

🥗 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟬/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗧𝗛+ 𝗟𝗶𝗳𝗲𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲: an AI planner for personalised yoga and food plans.
Ask an AI chatbot for a diet plan and you usually get a paragraph. You can’t track a paragraph.

🧩 The problem: people want a yoga and nutrition plan they can follow, log and adjust. AI gives them nice text, but an app can’t schedule, track or update a paragraph.

💡 The insight: AI output only becomes a product feature once it’s structured and checked.

🛠️ What I built: a planner whose plans arrive as structured data, so they show up as daily meal checklists with macros (protein, carbs, fat, fibre) and timed yoga sessions, not a wall of chat text.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• A fixed plan format the app can read. Anything else is rejected.
• Two AI steps: one drafts the plan, a second checks it.
• Built from real lists of yoga sequences and foods, not made-up options.
• The optional AI coach sits behind an on/off switch to keep costs under control.

⚖️ The trade-off: strict structure limits how creative the AI can be. Reliability wins.

📊 How I’ll measure success: plans generated, days logged per user, plans followed past week one and past 30 days, and the end goal: subscribers who renew.

title: Markets Pro
post:
Most trading tips only show you the wins. Almost nobody shows you the trades that lost money.

💹 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟭/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗣𝗿𝗼: a trading research engine for India, the US, China and Russia.
Its demo loses money on purpose, and that’s the most honest thing about it.

🧩 The problem: retail investors want strategies they can trust before risking real money, but many backtests show beautiful profit curves that quietly cheat. They peek at future prices (look-ahead bias), ignore taxes or skip settlement rules, and real money pays for the bug.

💡 The insight: the product isn’t trade ideas. It’s numbers you can trust.

🛠️ What I built: a research engine that tests long-term momentum and short-term swing strategies with each market’s real rules and costs.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Real costs per market: STT, stamp duty and GST in India, regulatory fees in the US, T+1 settlement in China.
• Every calculation is checked against hand-worked answers. One failure blocks the release.
• Paper trading only, with no broker connection. Trust comes before money.

⚖️ The trade-off: the demo runs on random data, so after realistic costs it should lose. If it made a profit, that would prove a bug.

📊 How I’ll measure success: the paper-trading record on real market data (returns after all costs, drawdown and win rate against a benchmark), strategies tested per user, and the end goal: users who trust the numbers enough to come back every day.

💬 Your turn: Have you ever trusted a backtest that turned out too good to be true?

title: MuseVibe Studio
post:
You can hum the song in your head. You just can’t explain it to a tool that gives you one empty box.

🎵 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟮/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗠𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗩𝗶𝗯𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗼: an AI music studio that turns a one-line idea into a full song.
Many AI music tools give you one text box and hope. This one helps you say what you mean.

🧩 The problem: many people know how a song should feel, but not the words for it: genre, tempo, vocal style, studio effects. So they type one vague line and get a random result.

💡 The insight: people know the feeling, not the vocabulary. The product should translate.

🛠️ What I built: describe your idea in plain words, like “a late-night drive in the Mumbai rain after a breakup”, and MuseVibe fills in the genre, tempo, mood, vocals and lyrics, ready to refine and generate.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• One line in, every field filled: genre, mood, energy, vocals and lyrics.
• AI help on every field, with Suggest and Enhance, so you can push one detail without starting over.
• Lyrics that respect language, including natural mixes like Hinglish.
• A single song or a full album, with a matching visual video if you want one.

⚖️ The trade-off: more fields on screen than a single text box, but every one is optional and pre-filled.

📊 How I’ll measure success: songs generated, share of songs finished, downloads and shares, returning creators, and the end goal: creators who come back to make their next song.

title: Kolab
post:
A small creator with a loyal audience can sell more than a big one with a bored audience. Most brands never get the data to tell them apart.

🤝 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟯/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗞𝗼𝗹𝗮𝗯: a two-sided platform for creators and the brands that pay them.
Brands stop paying for follower counts and pay on results from verified creators.

🧩 The problem: Indian creators run their business across a pile of apps, and brands still can’t tell which creators are real, so they pay for follower counts instead of results.

💡 The insight: both sides have the same problem. The tools and the trust live in different places.

🛠️ What I built: creators plan and schedule content, link every channel, launch a coupon storefront with affiliate codes and get paid. Brands discover verified creators and run commission deals.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Two-sided pricing: creators subscribe to Basic or Pro, brands partner on commission.
• Verification is the moat. Linked channels make a creator trustworthy to a brand.
• Built for India: mobile OTP and Aadhaar eKYC sign-in are designed in and run in demo mode until a licensed KYC partner is plugged in.

⚖️ The trade-off: prototype first. I’m proving the flow before paying for the expensive parts.

📊 How I’ll measure success: verified creators, brands onboarded, deals closed, sales through creator coupon storefronts, and the end goal: subscription and commission revenue.

title: Shoutout
post:
Booking a musician in India still runs on phone calls, forwarded numbers and “I’ll get back to you.”

🎤 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟰/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗼𝘂𝘁: one platform for independent musicians to find gigs, collaborators and auditions.
Every request becomes a “Shout” that someone answers, and that one idea runs the whole platform.

🧩 The problem: independent musicians find gigs in one place, collaborators in DMs and auditions somewhere else, and payment is informal at best.

💡 The insight: underneath every interaction is the same action. Someone asks, someone answers.

🛠️ What I built: one platform where every request, from a gig to a collab to an audition, is a Shout.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• One unit, many uses. 12 types of Shout are set up as configuration, so a new type doesn’t mean a new product.
• One matching engine for every type, so recommendations improve across the platform.
• Payments on double-entry accounting, because marketplaces die when payments break.
• Humans review auditions and disputes, where judgement matters.

⚖️ The trade-off: a general building block takes longer to design than a single gig board, but the platform can grow without being rebuilt.

📊 How I’ll measure success: Shouts posted, Shouts answered within 48 hours, bookings completed, payment volume through the platform, and the end goal: repeat bookings.

title: ANCHOR
post:
Many artists dream of releasing music every day. This one actually does, and it isn’t human.

🎧 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟱/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗔𝗡𝗖𝗛𝗢𝗥: an AI techno artist that releases a new track every single day.
It runs on an automated pipeline I built, around the clock, at ₹0.

🧩 The problem: an artist needs a steady stream of releases to grow an audience, and creators rarely fail for lack of talent. They fail at consistency.

💡 The insight: consistency can be automated, as long as quality and platform rules are built in.

🛠️ What I built: every day, ANCHOR writes a creative brief, generates an industrial techno track, checks its quality, masters it, designs the cover, cuts a Short, publishes everywhere with AI disclosure, and updates its website. Every Sunday it releases a weekly mix.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Zero cost as a constraint. Free compute and open-source models shaped the whole design.
• Quality gates check loudness (LUFS), clipping and tempo, so silent or broken tracks never ship.
• Built for platform rules. Every release changes tempo, key, sound, cover and visuals.
• Failure you can see. If a run breaks, the status turns red, and nothing posts twice.

📡 Where it publishes:
• YouTube @ANCHOR_AT: 167 videos so far, with 30 subscribers and growing
• Instagram @anchor_at2803: every release as a Reel

⚖️ The trade-off: zero cost means slower free models, so each release takes longer to make.

✅ Results so far: 167 videos published, at ₹0.

📊 How I’ll measure success: views, watch time, subscribers and listens per release, cost per release kept at ₹0, and the end goal: a growing audience that comes back for every drop.

title: JobHunt
post:
Job hunting means rewriting the same resume again and again, and hearing back from almost no one.

💼 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟲/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗝𝗼𝗯𝗛𝘂𝗻𝘁: a free AI agent that finds real job openings and tailors your resume to each one.
Without ever inventing experience you don’t have.

🧩 The problem: job hunting means endless open tabs and one resume sent everywhere. Tailoring each application takes hours, and many AI tools exaggerate to fill the gaps.

💡 The insight: the hard part isn’t finding openings. It’s tailoring each application without exaggerating.

🛠️ What I built: sign in with Google and search once. JobHunt pulls real openings from free public job boards, links one-click searches on LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor and Upwork, and writes a tailored resume and cover letter for each job.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Grounded only in what you give it. It matches your real experience to each job’s keywords and never invents any.
• Your profile stays in your own browser, not on my servers.
• Free, with no API key and no setup.

⚖️ The trade-off: free public job boards have fewer listings than paid feeds, but every listing is real.

📊 How I’ll measure success: searches run, applications sent per session, interviews per application, returning users, and the end goal: offers landed.

💬 Your turn: What’s the most time-consuming part of applying for jobs?

title: Books on Amazon
post:
Writing a book takes months. Formatting it, designing the cover and publishing every edition takes almost as long.

📚 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟳/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲: 4 thrillers and 3 kids’ drawing books, now on Amazon.
Written with an engine I built, and published in every format.

🧩 The problem: I wanted to test whether one person, with AI, can run a real publishing business. Publishing usually takes writers, editors, designers and months per book, and many self-published AI books are low quality and get ignored.

💡 The insight: AI can do the volume, but only quality gates make it a real product.

🛠️ What I built:
• The Watermark Files: an Indian conspiracy-thriller series under my own name. Books 1-4: The Palace Writer, The Stamp Vendor, The Second Inventory and The Devpur Deed. Lead: Ira Sahni, a document examiner from Delhi.
• Doodle Lane Studio: step-by-step drawing books for kids 6-9 (Christmas, cute animals, and things that go), promoted with a new drawing every day on Instagram @ai_at2803.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• A series, not one-offs. A recurring lead brings readers back for the next book.
• Quality gates: originality and plagiarism checks, plain-English style rules, and a chain of AI models so drafting never stalls.
• Every format, every store: Kindle, paperback and hardcover. Book 1 is ₹99 so new readers can try the series.

✅ Results so far: 7 books live on Amazon, and a new drawing Reel every day on @ai_at2803.

⚖️ The trade-off: zero ad spend means slower discovery. I’m growing it organically first.

📊 How I’ll measure success: books sold, Kindle pages read, readers who go from Book 1 to Book 2, reviews and ratings, and the end goal: royalties.

title: The Passion Table
post:
It’s 7 PM. Everyone’s hungry, nobody wants to cook, and ordering in again doesn’t feel right.

🍲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟴/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲: a daily home-style food service run from neighbourhood kitchens.
Subscribe, order on demand or reserve a table, so nobody at home has to be the one who cooks.

🧩 The problem: in working households in Indian cities, dinner means cooking after work, a cook who didn’t turn up, or another ₹400 delivery you regret by 9 PM. And the assumption that one person in the house, usually a woman, will handle it.

💡 The insight: restaurant food is a treat. Daily food needs to be home-style, reliable and decided once.

🛠️ What I built: the product end to end. Local “Eating Joints” cook fresh every day, and you choose how the food reaches you. It isn’t taking public orders yet.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Three ways to eat from one kitchen: a meal subscription, on-demand ordering with live tracking, or a reserved table.
• Choice without the daily decision. Subscribers pick one of three meals each day, and can pause, resume or change any time.
• Home-style, not restaurant-style: food built to be eaten five nights a week.

⚖️ The trade-off: this is the only product on this list with real-world operations, which makes it slower to scale than software.

📊 How I’ll measure success: subscribers, month-on-month retention, on-time deliveries, orders per household each week, and the end goal: profitable repeat orders.

💬 Your turn: Who decides what’s for dinner in your home?

title: Airpane
post:
Your phone screen is too small, your laptop is across the room and the TV is busy. What if the screen simply floated wherever you needed it?

🪟 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟭𝟵/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗔𝗶𝗿𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗲: an AR browser that makes any website float in your room.
No headset and no app. Just the phone, laptop and TV you already own.

🧩 The problem: AR headsets cost more than many phones, and many people will never buy one.

💡 The insight: the hardware for AR is already in people’s pockets: a phone camera and a laptop webcam.

🛠️ What I built: on a phone, the page stays pinned in your room. On a laptop, the webcam tracks your head so the page looks like a 3D hologram. On a TV, it catches pages you throw to it.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• A gesture people already know: pinch, swing and let go to throw a page to your TV. Your phone becomes the remote.
• No app needed on any device, including iPhones and smart TVs.
• Sites that block embedding open in a cloud browser that only switches on when enabled, so costs stay in check.

⚖️ The trade-off: browser-based AR is less precise than a headset, but it reaches everyone.

📊 How I’ll measure success: sessions, pages thrown to a TV per session, return visits, shares, and the end goal: people using it every week.

title: Games
post:
Remember when a game was just: open it and play? No download, no sign-up, no update to wait for.

🎮 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟮𝟬/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗚𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘀: 17 browser games I built from scratch in plain JavaScript and canvas.
No engine, no image files, no downloads and no sign-in. Open the page and play.

🧩 The problem: I wanted games that start the moment the page opens, on any phone, tablet or laptop, without a download or an account.

💡 The insight: if every road, pitch, crowd and car is drawn in code, a game loads instantly and works everywhere.

🛠️ What I built: a city to roam, a night race, a mountain-road bike race, rooftop football, two kinds of cricket, basketball, kite fighting, a tiffin run, carrom, a catch in the yard, rooftop squash, an auto through the bazaar, a rooftop platformer, kart racing, 5v5 paintball and rocket-car football.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• No engine and no image files. Everything is drawn in code as you play.
• Keyboard, mouse and touch on every game, so it plays the same on phone, tablet and desktop.
• Modes on every game, and your best scores saved on your device.

⚖️ The trade-off: drawing everything in code limits how realistic the art can look, in exchange for instant loading.

📊 How I’ll measure success: games played per visit, session length, return visits, and the end goal: players who come back to beat their best score.

• Every frame drawn in code, in a watercolour brush style.
• English voice-over, chapters and subtitles in a player that works in any browser.
• Dailies from the next film go up on the page as they’re made.

⚖️ The trade-off: a hand-painted, code-drawn look instead of photorealism.

📊 How I’ll measure success: plays, minutes watched, completion rate, shares, and the end goal: an audience waiting for the next film.

title: Prompter Cam
post:
Recording a video, you either look at the lens and lose your lines, or read your lines and look away from the lens.

🎥 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝟮𝟮/𝟮𝟯 · 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝗺: a teleprompter and camera in one browser tab.
Read your script while looking at the lens, and record in the same place.

🧩 The problem: recording a talking-to-camera video usually means juggling a script, a camera app and a recorder, and your eyes drift away from the lens.

💡 The insight: put the reading line right under the camera, and the record button in the same window.

🛠️ What I built: a browser teleprompter with your webcam and mic built in. Set the speed and text size, mirror the text, edit the script, and record takes at up to 4K.

🎯 Key product decisions:
• Keyboard controls: R to record, Space to scroll, arrow keys to nudge.
• Private by default. Recordings stay in your tab until you download them, and script edits stay in your browser.
• Coaching built in: a word count, an estimated read time, and tips on light, sound and framing before you record.

⚖️ The trade-off: no cloud storage, so closing the tab discards any take you haven’t downloaded.

📊 How I’ll measure success: takes recorded per session, takes downloaded, return visits, and the end goal: people recording their videos here instead of juggling three apps.

Don’t just read about my work. Question it.

🛠️ What I built: “Anchit LLM”, an assistant grounded only in my real work, which answers questions in a cloned version of my voice.

title: The workflow behind the series
post:
⚙️ You’ve just read 23 product stories, one every 6 hours.
Here’s the publishing workflow behind them, and why I built it.

🧩 The problem: builders ship, then go quiet. Writing about your work can take as long as building it, so many projects never get their story told.

💡 The insight: automate the repetitive part, and keep a human exactly where trust lives.

🛠️ What I built: a publishing workflow that keeps my approved posts in a private queue and publishes the next one every 6 hours, using LinkedIn’s official API.

🎯 The product decisions:
• Publish only. It never likes, comments on others’ posts, messages or connects. Every conversation stays human.
• A content guard checks every post before it goes out. Unfinished placeholders or broken formatting block it.
• I approve every post before it goes live.
• Built for failure. It never posts twice, a pause switch stops everything, and if a run breaks I get an email and the next day carries on.

It’s built the same way as ANCHOR, my automated pipeline that releases a techno track every day.

📌 The lesson: automation shouldn’t replace your voice. It should make sure you actually use it.

That’s the series. If one of these products sparked an idea, tell me in the comments or send me a DM. I read every one.
